title: Orchard and Clock
premise: In 1917, field nurse Emrys Vane secretly records the deaths officers leave off official ledgers, believing names deserve survival even when men don't. When a stranger delivers a letter in the unmistakable hand of Captain Aldous Wren—officially dead for eight months—she discovers the 'casualty' lists she's been keeping contain evidence of a supply-line fraud that killed hundreds, and Wren is alive, hiding, and willing to testify. Pursued by the officer who built the fraud, Emrys must smuggle her ledger and Wren's letter through three military checkpoints to a mail ship sailing on the morning tide. She loses the ledger at the final gate but has memorized every name, reciting them aloud on the dock until a war-correspondent passenger writes them down; the ship sails, the evidence reaches a tribunal, and Emrys survives to see Wren's name restored—choosing truth over the loyalty that nearly cost her everything.
about_author: Dominic Lockridge is a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing soldiers' letters in regional collections before turning to fiction. He writes historical novels about the people history files under 'miscellaneous.'

chapters.title: The Second Ledger
chapters.summary: Emrys Vane, POV. In a crowded field hospital, Emrys tends wounds by day and records omitted names in her hidden notebook by night. The emotional beat is quiet resolve: she has made a private covenant that no one dies unwitnessed, even if the army says otherwise.

chapters.title: A Stranger at the Ward Door
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. A mud-caked stranger, Tomas Bell, asks for her by name—a name no one should know. He carries a letter in Captain Aldous Wren's handwriting, a man she watched die on paper eight months ago. Beat: dread sharpening into curiosity.

chapters.title: Ink That Should Be Dry
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV, flashback woven in. She verifies the handwriting against old requisitions Wren signed and confronts the impossible: he lives. Bell warns that her ledger names men who died of 'misrouted' supplies. Beat: the personal becomes conspiratorial.

chapters.title: What the Quartermaster Counted
chapters.summary: Tomas Bell's POV. Bell explains the fraud: Major Corven Halloway diverted rations and morphine for profit, and Wren's reports threatened to expose him. Beat: the scale of the crime lands like a physical blow.

chapters.title: The Officer Who Smiles
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. Halloway himself tours the ward, charming and watchful, and pauses too long at her cot. She realizes he may already suspect the ledger exists. Beat: fear wearing a polite face.

chapters.title: Wren, Alive and Unwilling
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV, night journey to a coastal barn. She meets Wren: broken, guilt-ridden, ready to vanish rather than testify. She argues that his name can save the others. Beat: loyalty and truth begin their war inside her.

chapters.title: Bell's Price
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. Bell confesses he once carried Halloway's false manifests and is buying back his soul with this errand. Emrys must decide whether a guilty messenger can be trusted. Beat: uneasy alliance, forgiveness withheld.

chapters.title: The Raid on Ward Six
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. Soldiers search the hospital for 'stolen documents'; Emrys hides the ledger inside a dead man's belongings. A fellow nurse, Sister Idris, covers for her at real risk. Beat: loyalty given without being asked.

chapters.title: Three Checkpoints
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The plan is laid: the evidence must pass the rail depot, the causeway gate, and the harbor quay before the mail ship sails on the morning tide. Beat: a countdown begins, ticking under every scene.

chapters.title: Sister Idris's Choice
chapters.summary: Sister Idris's POV. Idris, who lost a son to the misrouted supplies, insists on carrying the ledger through the first checkpoint in a laundry cart. She is questioned, nearly broken, and passes. Beat: sacrifice that costs her post and safety.

chapters.title: The Rail Depot at Dusk
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. First checkpoint: Emrys and Bell bluff through an inspection by hiding the letter in a hymnal. Halloway's adjutant is present, watching faces rather than bags. Beat: terror disguised as routine.

chapters.title: What Emrys Owes
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV, reflective interlude on the night train. She rereads her ledger and admits why she keeps it: her brother's name was erased from a list years ago. Beat: the theme of inheritance—of names, debts, and grief—made explicit.

chapters.title: Betrayal on the Causeway
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. Bell's old accomplice spots him at the second checkpoint and offers him amnesty for naming the courier. Bell refuses, is arrested, and swallows nothing—he simply lies beautifully. Beat: loyalty chosen at personal ruin.

chapters.title: The Gate at Low Tide
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. The second checkpoint tightens; the ledger is nearly found in her medical satchel before Wren, disguised as a stretcher-bearer, creates a diversion. Beat: Wren's first act of courage, purchased with exposure.

chapters.title: Halloway Closes the Net
chapters.summary: Halloway's POV. The major, elegant and ruthless, orders the harbor sealed and offers Emrys a bribe through an intermediary: her brother's true death record in exchange for the ledger. Beat: temptation with a human face.

chapters.title: The Offer She Refuses
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. Emrys confronts the bribe—her deepest wound traded for her silence—and refuses, understanding that the ledger is her inheritance and her brother's only monument. Beat: the price of survival named and declined.

chapters.title: Wren Decides
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren, who could still flee to a neutral port, chooses to walk into the harbor office and sign a sworn statement, knowing it may be his death warrant. Beat: truth outweighing self-preservation at last.

chapters.title: The Third Checkpoint
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. At the quay, Halloway personally searches her. The ledger is seized and burned before her eyes; she is released, hollow, with hours until the tide. Beat: despair at the lowest point of the arc.

chapters.title: Every Name by Heart
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. In the dark, Emrys realizes the ledger was never the evidence—she is. She memorized every name, date, and manifest number. Beat: grief transmuted into ferocious purpose.

chapters.title: The Morning Tide
chapters.summary: Emrys and Wren's POV, alternating. On the dock, Emrys recites the ledger aloud while Wren signs his statement; war correspondent Nathaniel Quill writes every word as Halloway's men close in. Beat: the climax—witness made public, unstoppable.

chapters.title: What the Ship Carried
chapters.summary: Quill's POV, weeks later. The dispatch reaches London; a tribunal convenes; Halloway is arrested at his desk mid-signature. Bell is freed; Idris is reinstated. Beat: vindication arriving quietly, like weather.

chapters.title: Orchard and Clock
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV, epilogue. In a restored orchard, Emrys plants a tree for each name she carried, while a clock on the chapel wall marks the hour her brother died. She tends the living and keeps the count. Beat: peace earned, memory kept, inheritance honored.
